strengths: Novel and elegant concept: Applying Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) downsampling to the sequence dimension of KV caches in decoder-only LLMs is an intuitive, parameter-free approach to cache compression.

Strong empirical motivation: The analysis demonstrating that key and value representations concentrate their energy in low-frequency components in deeper Transformer layers provides a solid foundation for low-pass filtering.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors validate the method across language modeling perplexity (PG-19, Proof-pile), downstream multi-task long-context benchmarks (LongBench), synthetic retrieval (Needle-in-a-Haystack), and detailed latency/FLOPs profiling.

Implementation efficiency: Handling RoPE by caching un-RoPEd keys and re-indexing compressed states within the cache avoids positional extrapolation issues without architectural modifications or auxiliary neural compressor modules.
weaknesses: Fairness of baseline comparison on LongBench: FreqKV is evaluated after supervised fine-tuning (LoRA on LongAlpaca), whereas several compared baselines (such as SnapKV, PyramidKV, and LM-Infinite) are training-free, post-hoc KV eviction/compression methods. Evaluating FreqKV zero-shot or providing comparisons with fine-tuned baselines would provide a clearer picture of the compression mechanism's standalone benefit.

Relatively modest context length evaluation on downstream tasks: While perplexity is tracked up to 32K/64K, the downstream evaluations (LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack) only extend context to 8K for LLaMA-2 and 16K for LLaMA-3, which is relatively short compared to current long-context benchmarks that routinely evaluate at 32K–128K.

Analysis of recursive compression artifacts: Because early tokens undergo repeated rounds of low-pass filtering and IDCT reconstruction as the context grows, high-order compression artifacts may accumulate. A deeper theoretical or empirical analysis of distortion on early sequence information under repeated compression steps would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Novel application of frequency-domain compression to the KV cache of decoder-only LLMs: The observation that KV representations concentrate energy in low-frequency components along the sequence dimension in deeper layers provides an intuitive motivation for DCT-based compression.

Parameter-free compression mechanism: Unlike approaches that add auxiliary neural modules (e.g., Activation Beacon or convolutional adapters), FreqKV relies on standard DCT/IDCT operations, avoiding added architectural complexity.
Bypassing positional extrapolation issues: Compressing keys prior to applying RoPE and re-indexing them within the cache window cleverly avoids out-of-distribution RoPE embeddings.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The paper evaluates language modeling perplexity (PG-19, Proof-pile), retrieval (Needle-in-a-Haystack), and multi-task long-context understanding (LongBench), demonstrating competitive performance and negligible computational overhead (<1% decoding latency overhead).
weaknesses: Fairness of comparison in downstream benchmarks: In Table 2 (LongBench), FreqKV is benchmarked against training-free KV cache compression methods (SnapKV, PyramidKV, LM-Infinite). However, FreqKV requires fine-tuning on LongAlpaca. Comparing fine-tuned models directly against inference-only/zero-shot compression methods without emphasizing this difference or without comparing to fine-tuned context-extension baselines (e.g., Activation Beacon, LoCoCo) on LongBench is somewhat unfair.

Performance degradation on structured/symbolic domains: As shown in Table 1 on Proof-pile, FreqKV trails behind full-cache methods (LongLoRA) by a notable margin at 16K and 32K (e.g., 2.72 vs 2.50 PPL). Frequency-domain low-pass filtering naturally acts as a positional smoothing filter, which likely blurs precise, token-level symbolic dependencies required for math and formal proofs.

Information degradation under repeated iterative compression: Because compressed chunks are concatenated and compressed again in subsequent cycles, the earliest tokens undergo recursive low-pass filtering. A deeper analysis or ablation on how repeated DCT/IDCT cycles impact early token representations over very long sequences (e.g., >64K) is missing.

Limited model scale exploration: Experiments are restricted to 7B and 8B models (LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B); evaluating on larger scale models (e.g., 13B/70B) would further validate whether frequency concentration trends hold consistently across model capacities.

strengths: Interesting conceptual angle: The paper introduces a frequency-domain perspective to KV cache compression in decoder-only LLMs, supported by empirical observations that key and value activations concentrate energy in low-frequency components across deeper layers.

Parameter-free compression operator: Unlike architectural extension methods that require auxiliary compression networks (e.g., LoCoCo, Activation Beacon), FreqKV relies on standard DCT/IDCT operations, avoiding added parameters and substantial memory overhead.

Low computational and latency overhead: Because compression is performed in chunks rather than at every single decoding step, the added FLOPs and latency overhead are minimal (less than 1% decoding latency overhead compared to token dropping).

Competitive perplexity results: On language modeling benchmarks (PG-19, Proof-pile), the model maintains stable perplexity out to extended contexts (up to 32K/64K) while using a fraction of the full KV cache.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison on LongBench: The downstream evaluation in Table 2 compares FreqKV against post-hoc, training-free KV cache compression methods (SnapKV, PyramidKV, LM-Infinite). However, FreqKV undergoes supervised fine-tuning on LongAlpaca. It is unclear how much of the performance gain originates from the frequency compression mechanism versus the domain adaptation/SFT on long-context instruction data.

Lack of zero-shot / training-free evaluation: The paper does not report whether FreqKV can function without fine-tuning. An ablation showing the zero-shot degradation before LoRA adaptation is crucial to understanding whether the model's pre-trained attention representations naturally tolerate low-frequency truncation.

Information degradation under cascaded compression: In long sequences, early tokens undergo multiple iterations of DCT downsampling and IDCT reconstruction. While the paper shows Needle-in-a-Haystack results, there is visible retrieval degradation for needles placed at earlier positions (shallow depths), and the paper lacks a theoretical or empirical characterization of signal degradation under repeated non-orthogonal truncations.

Semantic implications of frequency truncation: Natural language tokens are discrete, non-stationary semantic units. While low-pass filtering hidden states smooths representations across tokens, the specific impact on token-level exact retrieval, entity tracking, or numerical reasoning needs deeper investigation beyond aggregate perplexity and QA scores.

strengths: Novel and elegant concept: Applying Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) along the sequence dimension of the KV cache to exploit the low-frequency concentration of LLM representations is an original and well-motivated approach for decoder-only architectures.

Clever workaround for RoPE out-of-distribution issues: Compressing the key representations prior to applying RoPE allows cached states to be indexed within the native positional window, effectively bypassing positional extrapolation failure modes without requiring complex position interpolation schemes.

Extensive experimental validation: The paper validates the approach across multiple complementary settings, including long-context language modeling (PG-19 up to 256K context), long-context understanding (LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack), and long-generation benchmarks (LongGenBench).

Thorough ablation studies: The authors provide detailed empirical analyses supporting key design choices, including low vs. high frequency retention, RoPE application order, the necessity of the sqrt(L/N) amplitude rescaling factor, and FLOP/latency overheads.
weaknesses: Fairness in baseline comparisons: FreqKV requires fine-tuning (LoRA plus trainable embedding and normalization layers on RedPajama/LongAlpaca), whereas many of the baselines in Table 3 (LongBench) and Table 4 (RULER)—such as SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, and ThinK—are strictly training-free inference-time eviction methods. The paper should clearly distinguish whether FreqKV can operate zero-shot/training-free, or compare against fine-tuned compression counterparts (e.g., LoCoCo, Activation Beacon) consistently across all benchmarks.

Information loss on high-frequency / symbolic information: As acknowledged in Appendix E on Proof-pile, discarding high-frequency components degrades performance on tasks with dense symbolic or numerical precision. In Table 4 (RULER at 16K), FreqKV experiences an accuracy drop (averaging 47.30% vs. 87.68% at 8K, with NIAH dropping to 25.47%), indicating that aggressive downsampling impacts fine-grained retrieval across long sequences.

Compounding error in iterative compression: Early tokens undergo multiple successive rounds of DCT, truncation, and IDCT. The manuscript would benefit from a more rigorous analysis of signal degradation and reconstruction error as a function of the number of iterative compression cycles applied to earlier context chunks.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated core observation: The paper provides clear empirical evidence that KV states in decoder-only LLMs exhibit strong energy concentration in the low-frequency domain along the sequence dimension across layers and attention heads.

Elegant and parameter-free compression mechanism: Utilizing DCT/IDCT for low-pass filtering along the sequence dimension is a neat, principled alternative to discrete token eviction and token merging. Furthermore, applying compression prior to RoPE indexing offers a clever workaround to avoid out-of-distribution positional extrapolation issues.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors evaluate FreqKV across diverse settings, including long-context perplexity extrapolation up to 256K tokens, long-context understanding (LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack), and extended generation (LongGenBench).

Thorough analysis and ablations: The manuscript includes helpful ablations on low vs. high frequency components, the necessity of the rescaling factor, retaining ratios, sink sizes, and computational overhead/FLOPs analysis.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding fine-tuning requirements: The abstract and introduction emphasize that FreqKV is 'parameter-free and architecture-agnostic', which may mislead readers into thinking it is a purely training-free inference-time KV cache compression method. However, FreqKV requires fine-tuning (LoRA on RedPajama or SFT on LongAlpaca). An ablation showing zero-shot (without fine-tuning) performance against inference-only baselines would clarify how much adaptation is strictly necessary.

Fairness of comparison beyond native context length: On RULER and Needle-in-a-Haystack at 16K (Table 4 and Figure 4), all baseline methods (SnapKV, FastKV, ThinK, etc.) collapse to nearly 0.0 because they are applied to LLaMA-3 without positional extension beyond its native 8K window. Meanwhile, FreqKV has been fine-tuned and re-indexes cached keys within the window. A fairer comparison at 16K would pair the KV eviction/merging baselines with standard positional interpolation/extrapolation methods (e.g., PI or YaRN).

Hardware implementation and kernel overhead: Although the theoretical complexity of DCT/IDCT via FFT is $O(N \log N)$ and latency results are reported, practical deployment of chunked frequency transforms during generation and prefill typically introduces non-negligible kernel launches and synchronization on GPUs compared to highly optimized FlashAttention kernels. A discussion on wall-clock serving throughput (tokens/second) in realistic serving frameworks (e.g., vLLM) would strengthen the practical impact.

strengths: Novel perspective: Utilizing Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to compress the KV cache along the sequence dimension offers an interesting and refreshing frequency-domain angle compared to standard token eviction or token merging.

Insightful empirical analysis: The spectral power analysis across layers (Figure 1 and Appendix B) provides compelling empirical motivation, showing that deeper transformer layers naturally concentrate energy into lower frequency bands.

Parameter-free compression operator: Unlike existing learned KV compression approaches (such as LoCoCo or Activation Beacon) that introduce extra model parameters, FreqKV relies on standard DCT/IDCT and rescaling, keeping the model architecture intact.
Iterative compression mechanism: The progressive compression design naturally reflects the asymmetric importance of recent versus distant context in autoregressive decoding.

Extensive experimental breadth: The authors evaluate on diverse benchmarks including language modeling (PG-19, Proof-Pile), long-context understanding (LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack), and long-context generation (LongGenBench), accompanied by FLOPs and latency profiling.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons on downstream benchmarks: FreqKV is fine-tuned (via LoRA on RedPajama or LongAlpaca), whereas nearly all compression baselines in Table 3 (SnapKV, PyramidKV, FastKV, GemFilter, ThinK, LaCache, D2O) are strictly training-free, post-hoc methods evaluated on frozen models. Comparing a fine-tuned model directly against training-free baselines confounds the benefit of adaptation with the compression method itself.

Misleading comparisons beyond the native context window: In Table 4 (RULER at 16K) and Figure 4 (Needle-in-a-Haystack beyond 8K), the authors report catastrophic failure of baselines on LLaMA-3-8B. However, these baselines are KV eviction methods designed to operate strictly within the native 8K window, not context extension methods. Demonstrating that an extended, fine-tuned model outperforms unextended models beyond their native training limit is an apples-to-oranges comparison.

Absence of zero-shot / training-free evaluation: The abstract describes FreqKV as a 'parameter-free and architecture-agnostic approach', but it actually requires LoRA fine-tuning. The paper does not show how FreqKV performs in a purely training-free setting, leaving it unclear whether the frequency compression is viable without task/corpus fine-tuning.

Ad-hoc handling of positional embeddings: Compressing key states prior to RoPE and then assigning sequential cache indices distorts relative token distances. While fine-tuning enables the model to adapt to this distortion, there is little theoretical or analytical justification for treating low-pass filtered continuous signals as discrete positional tokens.

Performance degradation on dense/symbolic domains: As shown in Table 9 (Proof-pile), FreqKV noticeably lags behind LongLoRA at longer lengths, showing that discarding high frequencies is detrimental when high-frequency local precision is essential (e.g., mathematics and code).
